people.abaza: Rear admiral, cousin and political ally of Alexander Bezobrazov. He belonged to the circle of Yalu timber-concession shareholders. The venture began commercially, but building fortifications under cover of logging tied it to Russia’s advance in Korea and pre-war rivalry with Japan.
people.aleksandr-iii: Emperor of Russia and father of Nicholas II. Sergei Witte’s rise and Russia’s rapprochement with France began under him. In 1891 Alexander III listened to the Marseillaise at Kronstadt, a striking moment in an autocratic empire’s alliance with a republic. French loans later helped finance Russia’s railway projects.
people.barabash: Russian general who proposed in 1887 that, in a war with China, forces should concentrate on Manchuria and, if unsuccessful, advance on Beijing. His memorandum appears in a study of “Yellow Russia” projects. It illustrates a military route to expanding Russian influence discussed before the Kwantung lease.
people.bezobrazov-pyotr: Vice admiral who temporarily commanded the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment. Under him, the detachment attacked Japanese transports in the Korea Strait in June 1904. He should not be confused with Alexander Mikhailovich Bezobrazov, the court-connected entrepreneur involved in the Yalu concession.
people.borodovskii: Orientalist who wrote Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan with Władysław Kotwicz. Published in St Petersburg in summer 1898, shortly after the Russian lease began, the 47-page booklet described the peninsula and its ports before Russian Dalny was built.
people.briner: Vladivostok merchant who obtained a Korean timber concession on the Yalu and Tumen rivers in 1896. It was later acquired by participants in the venture associated with Alexander Bezobrazov. Briner’s name marks the original business deal from which a political project developed.
people.chertkov: Publisher and friend of Leo Tolstoy. He helped publish the anti-war essay Bethink Yourselves! abroad after Russian newspapers rejected it. Chertkov sent the text to England, where it appeared in The Times in summer 1904. Tolstoy’s appeal to his contemporaries thus found readers beyond the Russian press.
people.denikin: Russian officer who sharply criticised Russia’s Far Eastern policy in 1908. He considered the Chinese Eastern Railway’s economic value small and its long route across foreign territory strategically disadvantageous; he called the troop presence in Manchuria an occupation. He chiefly blamed Witte. This judgment was made after defeat in the war.
people.dubasov: Russian admiral involved in the occupation of Kwantung. The overview of the two cities names him among the earliest leaders of Russia’s presence on the peninsula, before Subotich and Alekseyev. His name belongs to the opening chapter of Russian Port Arthur and Dalny.
people.essen: Naval officer who commanded the battleship Sevastopol during the final phase of Port Arthur’s defence. When siege artillery began shelling the ships in the inner harbour, he moved the battleship to White Wolf Bay. After repelling destroyer attacks, her crew scuttled her before the fortress surrendered.
people.georg-grecheskii: Greek prince and cousin of the future Nicholas II. He joined the Eastern journey at Piraeus and accompanied the heir in Japan. He should not be confused with Nicholas’s younger brother, Georgy Alexandrovich, who also began the journey but fell ill and returned home.
people.grodekov: Governor-General of the Amur region and a participant in debates over Manchuria’s future. In the memorandum quoted by the channel, he opposed both abandoning influence there and outright annexation. After the Russo-Japanese War, he warned of another possible conflict with Japan.
people.hodyakov: Historian who examined plans for Russian policy in Manchuria through military memoranda in the archives. His study of “Yellow Russia” underpins a channel article. It shows that advocates of annexation had no shared idea of how the territory would be governed.
people.ivanov-13: Lieutenant aboard Rurik who took command after the captain and senior officers died fighting Japanese cruisers. With her steering disabled, the ship could no longer escape. Ivanov ordered her scuttled to keep her from the enemy; the Japanese rescued surviving sailors. Ivanov the Thirteenth later became a rear admiral.
people.kirill-vladimirovich: Grand duke and cousin of Nicholas II. The Port Arthur overview connects him with the beginning of the Russian lease: on 16 (28) March 1898 he raised the Russian flag over Golden Hill. Russia and China had signed the convention leasing Liaodong’s southern tip the previous day.
people.kokovtsov: Russian finance minister, later chairman of the Council of Ministers. The account of Nicholas II compares his memoirs with Witte’s judgments. Kokovtsov portrayed the emperor as a decent man too susceptible to his entourage. This is testimony about the ruler’s character, rather than a complete explanation of the war’s causes.
people.kolchak: Naval officer and defender of Port Arthur. During the Russo-Japanese War he commanded the destroyer Serdity; his service aboard Diana in Stepanov’s novel is a fictional departure. Alexander Lysev used his notebook in researching the fortress’s everyday life.
people.kotvich: Orientalist who prepared the 1898 booklet Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan with Leonid Borodovsky. They described the newly leased territory, its geography and ports. The publication allows comparison between early impressions of Liaodong and what was subsequently built at Dalny and Port Arthur.
people.kulichkin: Author of a biography of Roman Kondratenko in the Lives of Remarkable People series, as well as historical fiction about Port Arthur. The channel reviews his book as a military biography with strong judgments about the general and his colleagues. The review helps separate the events from the author’s interpretation.
people.lenin: Bolshevik leader and author of The Fall of Port Arthur. He viewed the fortress’s surrender in relation to the political crisis of the autocracy. The channel compares this perspective with later Soviet accounts and changing interpretations of Russia’s defeat.
people.levitov: Journalist and ethnographer associated on the channel with the idea of “Yellow Russia”. He proposed a buffer colony between Lake Baikal and the Pacific, outlining it in a 1905 report. This was a project of its time, rather than the name of an administrative territory that actually existed.
people.linevich: Russian general who commanded a force in the allied advance on Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion. The channel notes that it was drawn mainly from the Kwantung garrison. His involvement connects the events of 1900 in northern China with Russia’s presence at Port Arthur.
people.lysev: Author of Russian Port Arthur in 1904: A History of Everyday Military Life. He studied food, housing, supplies and leisure among the garrison and civilians. Official returns and administrative records are compared with diaries and memoirs, revealing how the fortress lived between battles.
people.martin-kristofer: British author of an overview of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The channel suggests it as one way into the subject. Its review weighs the strengths of a coherent narrative against the limitations of a book written long before current research.
people.meidzi: Japanese emperor during Nicholas’s Eastern journey and the Russo-Japanese War. In the account of Ōtsu, he personally helped resolve the crisis after the attack on the Russian heir. Meiji is also used as an era name in Japanese publications and catalogues.
people.minaev: Author and presenter of MINAEV LIVE. His hour-long Russo-Japanese War episode moves from imperial pre-war policy through Port Arthur, Mukden and Tsushima to Portsmouth. The channel recommends it as a modern popular introduction; the site’s library preserves the video link.
people.molodyakov: Historian of Japan and author of studies of international relations and culture. The channel reviews his books on the Franco-Russian alliance and Russia’s rapprochement with Japan after the war. They connect Port Arthur’s history with diplomacy, loans and changing relations between former enemies.
people.myulberg-evgenii: Second lieutenant and defender of Port Arthur, father of the infant Mikhail Mühlberg. According to Dmitry Nikolayev’s archival research, discussed on the channel, he was wounded and awarded the Order of St George. The family’s story was reconstructed through documents and the child’s grave in Nagasaki’s Russian cemetery.
people.nazarenko: Naval historian whose lecture on the Russo-Japanese War is recommended by the channel. A central theme is hindsight: judging decisions made by people who did not yet know how the war would end. The lecture helps readers approach the defence without assuming defeat was obvious to everyone involved.
people.nikolaev-dk: Historian who reconstructs individual lives from archival documents. Using parish registers, he studied the family of the infant Mikhail Mühlberg, buried in Nagasaki. With Oleg Chistyakov, he checked the claim that Alexander Stepanov and his father had defended Port Arthur: archival research did not confirm their presence in the fortress.
people.panishchev: Author of The Crisis of Moral Consciousness in Russia and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The channel reviews it critically, examining how moral explanations of defeat relate to specific military events. This entry leads to that review; its judgments are those of the channel’s author.
people.poselyagin: Writer of the alternative-history series The Twins, including Ensigns of the Admiralty and Lieutenants of the Admiralty. The books are set around Port Arthur and the Russo-Japanese War. The channel discusses them as fiction that changes events and the lives of historical figures.
people.reitsenshtein: Naval officer who temporarily led the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment before Karl Jessen’s appointment. He appears in the history of its operations and in the review of Valentin Pikul’s Cruisers. These articles allow readers to compare the historical participant with his fictional portrayal.
people.rennenkampf: Russian general commanding a mounted force in Manchuria. The 1905 land-war album includes photographs of his Transbaikal Cossacks and the commander-in-chief’s visit. They show the Manchurian army in another theatre of war, far from besieged Port Arthur.
people.rozhestvenskii: Admiral who commanded the Second Pacific Squadron on its voyage to the Far East, ending at the Battle of Tsushima. The channel discusses him in its overview of the war and its review of an online account examining command decisions and later explanations of defeat.
people.ruzvelt: US president who mediated the end of the Russo-Japanese War. His involvement helped bring about the Portsmouth negotiations in 1905. The channel connects Roosevelt’s diplomatic role with Witte’s actions, Japan’s demands and the peace terms.
people.saginadze: Historian and author of A Reformer after the Reforms: S. Yu. Witte and Russian Society, 1906–1915. Her research underpins the article on Witte’s reputation after his retirement. It examines newspapers, satire, public expectations and political struggles conducted through the press.
people.shevchenko-av: Compiler of Anecdotes of the Russian Empire: The Russo-Japanese War, reviewed on the channel. The collection offers material on reputations and ways of making sense of the war. A joke conveys the attitudes of its teller and audience; by itself, it does not establish that an event occurred.
people.skitalets: Pen name of Stepan Petrov. The channel names him as the author of an early set of lyrics for Ilya Shatrov’s waltz On the Hills of Manchuria. The music was originally instrumental; its lyrics and their later variations form a separate history of its reception.
people.smirnov: Commandant of Port Arthur during the siege. This post should be distinguished from command of the Kwantung Fortified Region, held by Stessel, and the land defences, led by Kondratenko. The channel also discusses Smirnov’s dispute with Alexander Fok and their duel in 1908.
people.sozonov: Participant in the 1904 assassination of Interior Minister Vyacheslav von Plehve. The channel uses this episode to close its account of the minister and the remark about a “small victorious war” attributed to him. Sozonov’s later life involved penal servitude and protest against the punishment of political prisoners.
people.stalin: Soviet leader. The articles on remembrance compare the Bolshevik attitude towards the autocracy’s defeat with his 1945 speech after victory over Japan. This shows how the same historical event acquired different meanings in the political language of different years.
people.stark: Vice admiral commanding the Port Arthur squadron when war began. During the night of 27 January (9 February) 1904, Japanese destroyers attacked the outer roadstead, damaging Retvizan, Tsesarevich and Pallada. Commanders changed over the squadron’s subsequent history; this opening blow fell during Stark’s tenure.
people.suvorin: Publisher of Novoye Vremya. He recruited Mikhail Menshikov, whose Letters to My Neighbours appeared several times a week, and corresponded with Sergei Witte. His newspaper shows how debate about the war and ministers became part of the struggle for public opinion.
people.takahasi: Japanese financier and statesman. During the Russo-Japanese War, he helped secure foreign loans, including in London and New York. The channel connects his work with the question of why military victories did not spare Japan financial exhaustion or the need for peace.
people.togo: Japanese admiral who commanded the fleet in the Russo-Japanese War. The channel’s overview follows the naval campaign from the attacks off Port Arthur to Tsushima. His name connects fleet operations across battles often read as separate episodes.
people.trusov: Captain of the Vladivostok detachment’s cruiser Rurik. He was killed in action against Japanese cruisers; after the senior officers died, Konstantin Ivanov took command. Trusov also appears in Pikul’s Cruisers, the subject of a separate channel review.
people.tsuda-sandzo: Japanese policeman who attacked the Russian heir Nicholas with a sabre at Ōtsu in 1891. The attack cut short the Japanese leg of his Eastern journey and caused a diplomatic crisis. The channel treats it as an episode in the future emperor’s life, separately from the causes of the 1904 war.
people.tsysi: Qing empress dowager who influenced Chinese policy in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. She appears in the channel’s biography of Li Hongzhang and its account of the Boxer Rebellion. These articles explain the Chinese court’s position under pressure from foreign powers.
people.uhtomskii: Rear admiral who took command after Wilhelm Vitgeft died in the Yellow Sea battle. The principal Russian ships returned to Port Arthur, while others went to neutral ports and were disarmed. Command within the fortress later passed to Robert Viren.
people.viren: Rear admiral who succeeded Ukhtomsky in command of Port Arthur’s naval forces. In the final phase, guns were removed from ships for the forts and sailors went to land positions. After 203 Metre Hill was lost, ships remaining in the harbour came under accurately directed siege-artillery fire.
people.yaroslavskii: Bolshevik journalist and party historian who wrote a booklet on the Russo-Japanese War. The channel treats it as an example of Soviet explanations of the war through the Revolution of 1905. In this reading, military defeats mattered above all for their effect on the autocracy.
people.ayrapetov: Historian and author of On the Road to Collapse: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. The book connects military operations with diplomacy, finance and decisions in St Petersburg. The channel recommends it as a study of the whole war, grounded in documents, memoirs and correspondence.
people.akunin: Author of The Diamond Chariot, a novel about Erast Fandorin. Its two settings, Japan in 1878 and wartime Russia in 1905, are joined by a detective plot. The channel suggests it as a fictional introduction while maintaining the distinction between invention and the documentary history of intelligence.
people.gyubbenet: Chief surgeon of the Port Arthur fortress, whose work is described in the article on medical care during the siege. The channel highlights operations for abdominal wounds and the conditions in which casualties were treated. His name also appears in discussions of different ways to count garrison losses.
people.krig: Volunteer nurse who cared for the wounded during the defence of Port Arthur. According to the medical article retold on the channel, she reached a dressing station under fire during the fighting for 203 Metre Hill and received the Medal for Bravery. The episode forms part of the fortress’s medical history.
people.krivosheev: Editor of the statistical study Russia and the USSR in the Wars of the Twentieth Century, used in the article on the cost of defending Port Arthur. It compares troop strength, armaments, casualties and prisoners. The book’s different accounting categories cannot be combined into a single death toll.
people.gilyarovsky: Writer, reporter and witness to the Khodynka disaster. His account is used in the channel article on Nicholas II’s coronation. It places the Moscow events of 1896 alongside Li Hongzhang’s visit and the negotiations that opened the way for the Chinese Eastern Railway.
people.yurovsky: Commandant of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, tasked with carrying out the decision to execute the imperial family and their companions. Among the dead was Yevgeny Botkin, a doctor and veteran of the Russo-Japanese War. The channel explicitly notes uncertainty over the exact membership of the execution squad.
people.beloborodov: Chairman of the Ural Regional Soviet in 1918. The channel identifies its presidium as the body that decided to execute the imperial family. The story connects to the site through Nicholas II and Yevgeny Botkin, the doctor killed with the family.
people.goloschekin: Ural military commissar involved in deciding the Romanovs’ fate in summer 1918. The channel describes his journey to Moscow and discussions with Sverdlov. The material does not establish a direct written order from Moscow; conjecture about such an order should not be presented as a discovered document.
people.sverdlov: Chairman of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee in 1918. He appears in the Ipatiev House article in connection with discussions of the Romanovs’ fate and the later approval of the Ural Soviet’s decision. The article distinguishes these circumstances from the question of a direct written order from Moscow, which has not been found.
people.tretyakov: Commander of the 5th East Siberian Rifle Regiment, which defended the Jinzhou position in May 1904. The article on General Fok describes the dispute over unused reserves and the abandonment of the position. Tretyakov continued to challenge Fok publicly after the war.
people.grigorovich: Admiral and commander of the port of Port Arthur. At the surrender trial, he recalled that Fok’s appointment to command the land defences led the garrison to expect imminent capitulation. This participant’s testimony appears in the article on Fok’s disputed reputation.

geo.blagoveshchensk: City on the Amur opposite the Chinese bank. Qing troops shelled it during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900. In response, Russian authorities drove Chinese residents into the river; thousands died. The episode shows that the conflict reached beyond Beijing and Manchuria into Russia’s borderlands.
geo.chemulpo: Korean port, now Incheon. On 27 January (9 February) 1904, the cruiser Varyag and gunboat Koreets fought a Japanese squadron here. Back in port, Varyag was scuttled and Koreets blown up. The battle occurred on the same day as the first clash of the main forces off Port Arthur.
geo.dalnii: Russian commercial city and port built by the Chinese Eastern Railway Company from the late nineteenth century on Dalian Bay. It became Dairen under Japanese rule and is now Dalian. It should be distinguished from Port Arthur: the two cities developed for different purposes on different bays.
geo.golubinaya-buhta: Bay west of Port Arthur considered suitable for a Japanese landing in 1904. Concern for this sector explains its appearance on a satirical postcard that spring. The hindsight article compares the postcard with the defenders’ expectations before the siege had run its course.
geo.harbin: City and railway junction in Manchuria that grew during construction of the Chinese Eastern Railway. Harbin was besieged during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900, and the railway attacked. Its history connects with Dalny through the transport system linking inland Manchuria with the sea.
geo.koreya: The Korean peninsula was a principal focus of Russian-Japanese rivalry before the war. The channel examines diplomatic interests, the Yalu concession and the opening of hostilities. It supplies the regional setting of a conflict extending far beyond Port Arthur.
geo.kvantun: Historical name for the southern part of the Liaodong peninsula leased by Russia in 1898, including Port Arthur and Dalny. The lease rights passed to Japan after the war. Kwantung should not be confused with Guangdong province in southern China.
geo.kvzhd: The Chinese Eastern Railway linked Russia’s railway network through Manchuria. Its southern branch reached Kwantung, and the railway company built Dalny. The channel considers it as a transport project, financial enterprise and subject of international politics.
geo.lyaodun: Peninsula in northeastern China, with Dalian and Lüshun near its southern tip. Its geography shaped the ports and the land approaches to Port Arthur. Kotwicz and Borodovsky’s 1898 booklet describes it before construction of Russian Dalny began.
geo.lyaoyan: Manchurian city near which a major Russian-Japanese battle took place in 1904. Surrounding sorghum fields obstructed observation and concealed troop movements; plants had to be cut down in front of positions. Liaoyang’s story shows how unfamiliar terrain changed established ways of fighting.
geo.manchzhuriya: Historical region in northeastern China. The Chinese Eastern Railway, Russia’s military presence and rivalry with Japan made it a principal arena of the conflict. The channel discusses both actual events and plans for the region’s future, including the unrealised “Yellow Russia”.
geo.mukden: Historical name of Shenyang. A major battle between the Russian and Japanese armies took place around Mukden in 1905. The site considers it through war overviews, studies of everyday military life and memoirs. This was the Manchurian front, rather than part of the Port Arthur fortress.
geo.otsu: Japanese city where the policeman Tsuda Sanzō attacked the Russian heir Nicholas in 1891. The channel examines the attack, the Japanese court’s response and the end of the journey. The episode preceded the war by more than a decade.
geo.pekin: Capital of the Qing empire. The channel connects Beijing with the Boxer Rebellion, the siege of the Legation Quarter and the advance of the Eight-Nation Alliance in 1900. Russian units for the operation were drawn in part from Kwantung.
geo.port-artur: Historical European name for Lüshun; the Japanese reading is Ryojun. A Russian naval base and fortress stood here in 1898–1905. Lüshun is now part of Dalian, but historical Port Arthur and the commercial city of Dalny were separate towns.
geo.portsmut: American city whose name is associated with the 1905 peace treaty between Russia and Japan. President Theodore Roosevelt mediated the negotiations. The channel examines the financial exhaustion of both sides, Witte’s actions and the transfer of lease rights to Kwantung.
geo.sahalin: Island in the Russian Far East whose southern half passed to Japan under the Treaty of Portsmouth. The articles on Witte discuss this concession alongside Japan’s abandonment of an indemnity and the negotiator’s subsequent reputation, including his nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”.
geo.shahe: Manchurian river that gave its name to the battle of October 1904. Shahe fighting and Putilov Hill occupy a central place in the commander-in-chief’s headquarters photographic album. Alongside battle pictures are dugouts, prisoners and the field army’s everyday life.
geo.shanhaiguan: Coastal pass and fortress at the eastern end of the Great Wall. It is the pass in Guandong, “east of the pass”, rendered in Russian as Kwantung. Originally, the Chinese term covered a much larger area than the southern Liaodong territory leased by Russia.
geo.sopka-putilovskaya: Height near the Shahe, taken by Russian troops in October 1904 and named after Major General Putilov. A series in the 1905 album shows it from the Japanese side, prisoners, captured guns, the general’s dugout and even a shell bursting on the hill. These are Manchurian army positions, rather than a Port Arthur fort.
geo.tsusima: Strait between Japan and the Korean peninsula, associated with the Battle of Tsushima in 1905. The defeat of the squadron arriving from the Baltic was the last major event of the naval war. In the channel’s overviews, it leads into the peace negotiations.
geo.tszinchzhou: Town and isthmus on the land approach to Kwantung. In May 1904, the position blocking the Japanese advance towards Dalny and Port Arthur was abandoned. The channel examines the battle through Tretyakov’s regiment, Fok’s reserves and naval support.
geo.uglovaya-gora: One of the heights on Port Arthur’s approaches. Kondratenko sought stronger garrisons here and on neighbouring Dagushan to hold the forward positions and buy time for the fortress. Heavy fighting later engulfed the area; the hill’s location should be checked against a historical plan.
geo.ulsan: Area off the Korean coast where the Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment fought Kamimura’s ships in 1904. Rurik sank, while Rossiya and Gromoboi returned damaged. The site discusses the battle in the detachment’s history and the review of Cruisers.
geo.vafangou: Area of a land battle in 1904, associated with modern Wafangdian. Here Yevgeny Botkin treated wounded men under shrapnel, carried them and gave them his horse. His Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War shows the battle through medical care as well as staff decisions.
geo.vladivostok: Russian Pacific port and base of a separate cruiser detachment during the war. Its ships attacked Japanese sea communications. Vladivostok also appears in Dalny’s story through Vladimir Sakharov, an engineer who had previously worked on its commercial port.
geo.volchi-gory: Heights on Port Arthur’s approaches, where Russian troops suffered a setback in July 1904 before retreating to the fortress. Afterwards Kondratenko issued an order explaining the enemy’s superiority in men and artillery, and reminding soldiers that defence behind forts and concrete casemates would be different.
geo.yalu: River forming the border between China and Korea. The channel connects it with the timber concession, Bezobrazov’s circle and military operations in 1904. Commercial interests, diplomatic rivalry and the opening land campaign meet at this geographical junction.
geo.zheltoe-more: Sea bordering China and the Korean peninsula. Particularly important to Port Arthur’s history is the battle of 28 July (10 August) 1904, in which squadron commander Wilhelm Vitgeft was killed. The main Russian force returned to Port Arthur afterwards.
geo.moskva: Moscow’s Khodynka Field was the scene of a disaster during Nicholas II’s coronation celebrations in 1896. The channel examines the event’s organisation, Gilyarovsky’s testimony and the court’s response. Li Hongzhang was in Moscow at the same time, negotiating a Russian-Chinese alliance.
geo.ekaterinburg: City where Nicholas II, his family and their companions were killed in the Ipatiev House in 1918. Among them was Yevgeny Botkin, a doctor and author of memoirs of the Russo-Japanese War. The site explores this connection in its account of the family and the doctor.
geo.nikko: Japanese city whose temples Vasily Vereshchagin painted during his autumn 1903 visit. These works preceded his final journey: in spring 1904 he went to Port Arthur and died aboard Petropavlovsk. The artist’s article places peaceful Nikkō views beside his reflections on war.
geo.transsib: The Trans-Siberian Railway linked European Russia with the Far East. The Chinese Eastern Railway through Manchuria formed part of the development of this connection. For Port Arthur and Dalny, the railway meant access to the empire’s interior and a means of supply.
geo.iokogama: Japanese port where part of Boris Akunin’s The Diamond Chariot takes place. The channel’s review connects Yokohama in 1878 with Fandorin’s early experiences of Japan. This is a fictional setting; the novel’s events are not a documentary history of the city.
geo.svistov: Bulgarian town on the Danube, also called Sistova in Russian sources. Alexander Fok first won military distinction here in the war of 1877; his later life and burial are connected with the same area. On the channel, Svishtov links the beginning and end of the general’s life.
